name: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema

clinicalPearls: A distinctive drug eruption with symmetrical erythema of the gluteal/perianal area and the major flexures
The gluteal V-shaped erythema gives the historical name baboon syndrome
It occurs after systemic exposure to a drug, without prior sensitisation at those sites
There are typically no systemic symptoms and no mucosal involvement
Common culprits include beta-lactam antibiotics and other systemic drugs
It resolves on stopping the culprit drug and has a benign course
reference.pathophysiology: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is a T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a systemically administered drug (or occasionally systemically absorbed contact allergen). For reasons that are not fully understood, the reaction localises symmetrically to the gluteal region and flexures. The immune response produces the characteristic well-demarcated erythema without the systemic features or mucosal involvement of more severe cutaneous adverse reactions, and it settles when the drug is withdrawn.
additionalInvestigations: Drug history correlating onset with a systemic drug
Clinical recognition of the symmetrical flexural distribution
Patch or drug testing where confirmation is needed
Exclusion of intertrigo and inverse psoriasis
redFlags: Systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement suggesting a more serious reaction
Features suggesting a severe cutaneous adverse reaction
Failure to resolve after stopping the drug
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, clearing within days to a couple of weeks after the culprit drug is discontinued.
pitfalls: Confusing it with intertrigo or inverse psoriasis
Failing to identify the systemic drug trigger
Not documenting the culprit for future avoidance
